title: Reliability patterns: circuit breakers, graceful degradation, health checks
story:
The patterns in this lesson are well known and easy to list. The harder question, and the one worth building the lesson around, is how you would know whether any of them works.

Start with the patterns, briefly, because they answer the failure modes from two lessons ago. A circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that is failing, so callers fail fast instead of queueing against something that cannot answer — it converts a cascade into a local degradation, and its interesting state is the half-open one where it lets a trial request through to find out whether to close again. Graceful degradation means deciding in advance which parts of a response are essential and which can be dropped, so that a recommendation service being down costs recommendations rather than the page. Health checks report whether an instance should receive traffic, and the trap is that a check which only proves the process is alive will keep a broken instance in rotation, while one that checks every dependency will take the whole fleet out when one shared dependency wobbles.

Now the part that matters. Basiri and colleagues argued in 2016 that modern software-based services are distributed systems with complex behaviour and failure modes, and that verifying reliability requires experimentation rather than reasoning alone. That claim is the reason this lesson is not a list. You cannot reason your way to knowing whether your circuit breaker trips correctly under a real partial failure, because the behaviour you are asking about emerges from the interaction of parts.

Their method has four steps and is worth following exactly. Define the steady state of the system to set a baseline for normal behaviour. Hypothesise that this steady state will continue in both the control and the experimental groups. Introduce variables reflecting real-world events such as server crashes, disk malfunctions or severed network connections. Then try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference between the groups. If the steady state is hard to disrupt, the system is robust; if there is a weakness, you have something to fix.

The choice of steady-state metric is the detail most people get wrong, and their example corrects it. The canonical measure is the rate at which customers press play on a streaming device — streams per second. That is a business metric, not a technical one, and the paper notes business metrics are often better suited to measuring customer experience. Which follows: your instance-level graphs can all look healthy while nobody can complete the thing they came to do, and a technical steady state would have told you nothing was wrong.

problem.name: Verified reliability
problem.shape: A system has mechanisms intended to survive failure, and nobody knows whether they work because the failures they address have not occurred yet.
tell: a reliability mechanism has never fired in production
health checks pass while users cannot complete anything
a fallback path exists and has never been executed
confidence in resilience rests on design review rather than evidence
problem.move: Define normal as a measurable quantity, preferably one describing what users accomplish rather than what servers report. Hypothesise it survives a specific injected fault, inject that fault with a bounded blast radius, and compare against a control. Treat a mechanism that has never fired as untested rather than as working.
problem.invariant: Whether a reliability mechanism works is an empirical question about interacting parts, so it is settled by experiment and not by design review.
problem.breaks: The experiment must run where the behaviour is real, which means production, which means the practice is only as safe as the blast radius you can bound. And defining normal as a single number is genuinely hard — choose a technical metric and you can pass the experiment while users are failing.

cost.time: building the ability to inject faults and to stop an experiment quickly, before any experiment is worth running
cost.space: none, beyond the control group's share of traffic
cost.beats: design review, which cannot predict emergent behaviour, and waiting for real incidents, which teaches the same lessons at a worse moment and without a control group

worked.problem: What would you measure to know whether a reliability mechanism actually works?
worked.reasoning:
Something that describes what users are accomplishing, measured against a control, while a specific fault is deliberately present — and if the mechanism has never fired, I would start from the assumption that it does not work.

The reason for that starting assumption is the argument that modern services are distributed systems with complex behaviour and failure modes, so verifying reliability requires experimentation rather than reasoning alone. A circuit breaker is code that has a configuration, a fallback path and a set of conditions under which it trips. Whether it trips correctly under a real partial failure depends on how the parts interact, and interactions are exactly what design review cannot settle.

So the method. Define the steady state as a baseline for normal behaviour. Hypothesise it will continue in both the control and experimental groups. Introduce variables reflecting real-world events — server crashes, disk malfunctions, severed network connections. Then try to disprove the hypothesis by looking for a difference between the groups. The framing as disproof is deliberate: you are not demonstrating resilience, you are attempting to break it and reporting whether you managed.

The metric choice is where I would spend the effort, because it is where this usually goes wrong. The canonical example is the rate at which customers press play — streams per second — which is a business metric rather than a technical one, and the paper notes business metrics are often better suited to measuring customer experience. That correction matters because instance-level graphs can be uniformly green while nobody can finish what they came to do. Processor usage, memory and instance counts describe your fleet. Completed checkouts, successful sign-ins and started playbacks describe whether the system is doing its job.

For the specific mechanisms, the fault has to match the claim. For a circuit breaker, make the dependency slow rather than absent, because slow is the case that fills queues and the case breakers exist for, and confirm callers fail fast while the steady-state metric holds. For graceful degradation, remove the non-essential dependency and verify the essential path completes, which also verifies your list of what is essential. For health checks, verify both directions: a genuinely broken instance leaves rotation, and a wobble in one shared dependency does not remove the entire fleet.

Two things I would insist on before running anything. A control group, because without one you cannot distinguish the effect of your fault from whatever else was happening. And a bounded blast radius with a fast stop, because the experiment must run where the behaviour is real and that means the practice is only as safe as your ability to end it.

problem.practice: Pick one reliability mechanism in your system and find out whether it has ever fired in production. Then write the steady-state metric you would use to test it — and check whether that metric describes your servers or your users. Finally, name the fault you would inject and how you would stop the experiment.

beats.broke: A system made of many parts has failure modes nobody enumerated, and the ones that matter are discovered during incidents rather than during design.
beats.fix: Stop reasoning about failure and start inducing it — define what normal looks like as a measurable quantity, hypothesise it survives a specific injected fault, and look for a difference against a control.
beats.cost: The experiment has to run where the behaviour is real, so the practice is only as safe as the blast radius you can bound — and defining normal as a number is harder than it sounds.

interview.q: What would you measure to know whether a reliability mechanism actually works?
interview.trap: Choosing a technical metric. Instance graphs can be uniformly green while nobody can complete what they came to do — the canonical steady-state measure is a business metric, because those are better suited to describing customer experience.
